newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium facing severe drought, no relief in sight.
newsitem.headline: Belgium facing severe drought, no relief in sight.

text.p: Belgium is suffering one of the longest droughts on record, and there is no quick relief in sight, according to the Royal Meteorological Institute.
"Since July 1995 we have an accumulated rainfall deficit of 255 litres per square metre (10 inches)," statistician Marc Vandiepenbeek said in an interview.
"Over the period we have had 1,123 litres per square metre (44.2 inches) against the 1,378 litres (54.2 inches) we would normally have expected," he added.
Not since the 1800s had there had been anything approaching such a large accumulated deficit, he said.
In the past 22 months, 16 had significant rainfall shortfalls, five had been slightly above average and one -- August 1996 -- had been substantially above average.
This month alone the country has only received 0.2 inches of rainfall compared with the normal 2.1 inches.
Since the weekend firemen have been damping down bush fires south of Antwerp started by a discarded cigarette.
Last August Belgium suffered major flooding as cloudburst followed cloudburst to make the month the wettest since 1833.
"But much of that simply evaporated, more was absorbed by plants and the rest went into the rivers," Vandiepenbeek said. "The ground itself got little benefit."
He said the best type of rain was long, steady showers in the autumn and winter when plants were dormant. In this way the soil was able to absorb the moisture and store it.

The best months for that, he said had been in November last year and, to a lesser extent, in February this year -- although most of the rain in February fell on frozen ground and was therefore wasted.
Some rain is forecast in coming days, but Vandiepenbeek said it would take many months of steady rainfall to recoup the deficit, and there was no end in sight to the drought.
"It is not up to me to say what the negative consequences of this drought will be, but it is obvious that the lower the water levels, the higher the concentration of pollutants," Vandiepenbeek said.
Farmers are suffering as their fields turn to dustbowls and their crops wither.
But they are also facing another threat as clear skies and cold northerly winds bring nightly frosts that attack buds and fruit.
